sections.title: 1. Primary Market: Purpose, Participants, and the Capital-Raising Process
sections.overview: The primary market is where issuers raise capital by selling newly created securities directly to investors, with proceeds flowing to the issuer. Investment bankers structure the offering, underwriters distribute it, and the Securities Act of 1933 governs the registration and disclosure framework. The primary market converts issuer capital needs (debt or equity) into investable securities.
key_concepts: Issuer: corporation, municipality, or government raising capital; receives net proceeds.
Investment banker / underwriter: advises issuer on structure, price, timing; assumes distribution risk under firm commitment.
Syndicate: group of underwriters sharing distribution risk; led by the managing/lead underwriter (book-running manager).
Selling group: broker-dealers who help sell shares but bear no underwriting liability.
Municipal advisor: fiduciary to municipal issuers (separate from underwriter role).

Methods of distribution: (a) Firm commitment — underwriter buys entire issue and resells (capital at risk); (b) Best efforts — underwriter acts as agent, returns unsold shares; (c) All-or-none (AON) — entire issue must sell or deal cancelled; (d) Mini-max — minimum must sell before any proceeds released.

Types of offerings: IPO (issuer's first public sale); Follow-on / additional primary offering (issuer sells new shares post-IPO); Secondary offering (existing large holders sell — proceeds to them, not issuer); Combined / split offering (mix of primary and secondary).
Public vs. private offering: public requires registration under the 1933 Act unless exempt; private uses exemptions (Reg D, Reg A, Rule 147, etc.).
Shelf registration (Rule 415): issuer registers securities once and sells in tranches over time (up to 3 years for most issuers), allowing rapid market access.
Tombstone ad: limited announcement permitted during registration; identifies issue, price, syndicate.
Indication of interest (IOI): non-binding investor expression during cooling-off period; not a sale.
rules: Securities Act of 1933 §7 — registration statement content (Schedule A for corporate, Schedule B for foreign government); experts must consent in writing to being named.
Securities Act of 1933 §8(a) — registration becomes effective on the 20th day after filing unless SEC accelerates; amendments restart the clock unless filed with SEC consent.
Securities Act of 1933 §8(b) — SEC may issue refusal order if statement is incomplete/inaccurate on its face.
Securities Act of 1933 §8(d) — SEC may issue stop order suspending effectiveness for material misstatements/omissions.

Securities Act of 1933 §10 — prospectus content; §10(a) final prospectus; §10(b) preliminary/summary prospectus; prospectus used more than 9 months after effective date must contain information dated within 16 months.
Securities Act of 1933 §23 — SEC neither approves nor disapproves securities; misrepresenting SEC "approval" is unlawful (basis for the no-approval disclaimer on prospectuses).
17 CFR 230.431 — summary prospectuses permitted.
17 CFR 230.164 — post-filing free writing prospectuses permitted in registered offerings (supplements §10 prospectus).
formulas: Underwriting Spread = Public Offering Price − Proceeds to Issuer per share
Spread Components: Manager's Fee + Underwriting Fee + Selling Concession (largest portion to seller of record)
Net Proceeds to Issuer = (Shares Sold × POP) − Total Underwriting Spread − Issuance Expenses
mnemonics: "MUS" — spread = Manager / Underwriter / Selling concession (smallest to largest typically: Manager < Underwriter < Selling concession).
"FBAM" — Firm commitment, Best efforts, All-or-none, Mini-max (distribution methods).
"20-and-out" — §8(a) default cooling-off = 20 days to effectiveness.

sections.title: 2. The Registration Process & Timeline (Securities Act of 1933)
sections.overview: An issuer making a non-exempt public offering must register with the SEC and file a registration statement that becomes the prospectus delivered to buyers. The process runs in three phases — pre-filing, cooling-off, and post-effective — each with strict communication rules. SEC review never constitutes approval of the security's merits.
key_concepts: Pre-filing period: no offers or sales permitted ("quiet period"). Issuer and underwriters negotiate the letter of intent.
Filing date: registration statement (typically Form S-1) filed with SEC.

Cooling-off period: minimum 20 calendar days under §8(a); SEC may accelerate. During cooling-off: NO sales; permitted activities include preliminary prospectus (red herring), tombstone ads, indications of interest, due diligence meetings.
Red herring (preliminary prospectus): omits final POP and effective date; bold red legend states it is not an offer to sell. Must be delivered to anyone receiving an IOI.
Due diligence meeting: syndicate verifies disclosures with issuer prior to effectiveness.
Effective date: SEC declares registration effective; sales may begin. Final prospectus must be delivered no later than confirmation of sale.
Aftermarket prospectus delivery (Rule 174): IPOs — 25 days if listed on exchange/Nasdaq, 90 days otherwise; follow-on offerings of reporting issuers — generally none if exchange-listed.
SEC deficiency letter: requests amendments; does not stop the offering but tolls effectiveness until cured.
Stop order (§8(d)): SEC suspends a registration already effective for material misstatement/omission.
Refusal order (§8(b)): issued pre-effectiveness within 10 days of filing if statement is incomplete on its face.
rules: Securities Act of 1933 §7 — registration statement contents and expert consents.
Securities Act of 1933 §8(a),(b),(c),(d) — effectiveness, refusal order, post-effective amendments, stop order.
Securities Act of 1933 §10 — prospectus contents; 9-month / 16-month staleness rule.
Securities Act of 1933 §23 — no SEC approval; unlawful to represent otherwise.
17 CFR 230.164 — free writing prospectus rules apply after filing.
mnemonics: Three-phase timeline: "Pre-File → Cool-Off → Post-Effective" = "Quiet → Red Herring → Final."
"No Sales, No Mail, No Money" — what is prohibited during the cooling-off period (no sales, no advertising beyond tombstone, no funds accepted).
"9-and-16" — prospectus older than 9 months must use info ≤ 16 months old (§10(a)(3)).

sections.title: 3. Exempt Securities & Exempt Transactions
sections.overview: Certain securities and transactions are exempt from the registration and prospectus requirements of the 1933 Act, although antifraud provisions still apply. Exemptions reduce capital-raising friction for governments, banks, small issues, and private placements.
key_concepts: Exempt securities (issuer-based): U.S. Treasuries and agency securities; municipal securities; securities of domestic banks (not BHCs); commercial paper with maturity ≤ 270 days; non-profit (religious/charitable/educational) issues; small business investment company (SBIC) securities; securities issued by common carriers regulated by the ICC.

Regulation A — small/medium offerings exempt from full registration: Tier 1 up to $20M / 12 months; Tier 2 up to $75M / 12 months (Tier 2 requires audited financials and ongoing reporting; preempts state blue-sky review).

Regulation D — private placements: Rule 506(b) — unlimited accredited investors + up to 35 non-accredited sophisticated investors; NO general solicitation. Rule 506(c) — unlimited accredited only; issuer must take reasonable steps to verify; general solicitation permitted.

Accredited investor (17 CFR 230.215 / Rule 501): natural person with income > $200K ($300K joint) for the last two years with expectation of same, OR net worth > $1M excluding primary residence; also includes holders in good standing of Series 7, 65, 82; knowledgeable employees of private funds; certain family offices/clients; and institutional categories (banks, registered investment companies, employee benefit plans > $5M, etc.).
Rule 147 / 147A — intrastate offering exemption: offering confined to single state where issuer is doing business; resale restrictions apply within 6 months.
Regulation S — offers/sales made outside the United States.

Rule 144 — safe harbor for resale of restricted (private placement) and control (affiliate) securities: 6-month holding period for reporting issuers (12 months non-reporting); volume limits for affiliates = greater of 1% of outstanding shares or average weekly trading volume over prior 4 weeks; Form 144 filed if sales exceed 5,000 shares or $50,000 in 90 days — filing must be electronic via EDGAR.
Rule 144A — resale of restricted securities to Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs — institutions owning/investing ≥ $100M in securities); creates liquid institutional market for private placements.
Rule 145 — reclassifications, mergers, consolidations, and asset transfers treated as offers/sales requiring registration unless exempted.
rules: 17 CFR 230.144 — Rule 144 resale safe harbor; Form 144 filed electronically on EDGAR (mandatory since April 13, 2023).
17 CFR 230.144A — private resales to QIBs.
17 CFR 230.145 — reclassifications/mergers as sales.
17 CFR 230.147 — intrastate offering exemption.
17 CFR 230.215 — accredited investor definition.
Blue-sky laws (state registration) — generally still apply unless preempted (e.g., Reg A Tier 2, covered securities).
formulas: Rule 144 Affiliate Volume Limit = MAX(1% of outstanding shares, Average weekly trading volume of prior 4 weeks)
Form 144 trigger = Sales > 5,000 shares OR > $50,000 in any 90-day period
mnemonics: "BUMS-C" exempt issuers — Banks, U.S. government, Municipals, Small business (SBIC), Commercial paper ≤ 270 days.
"6-and-12" — Rule 144 holding: 6 months reporting issuer, 12 months non-reporting.
"200/300/1M" — accredited income $200K single / $300K joint / $1M net worth (ex-residence).
"506(b) = Buddies (no solicitation)"; "506(c) = Commercials OK (general solicitation, accredited only)."

sections.title: 4. Offering Documents & Disclosure Requirements
sections.overview: The prospectus is the primary disclosure document delivered to investors in a registered offering; municipal issuers use an Official Statement; mutual funds and other products have analogous documents. Disclosure is the foundation of investor protection under the 1933 Act.
key_concepts: Final (statutory) prospectus — §10(a): must be delivered no later than the confirmation of sale; contains POP, effective date, final terms.
Preliminary prospectus / red herring — §10(b): used during cooling-off for IOIs; omits POP and effective date.
Summary prospectus — Rule 431: condensed version permitted in lieu of full statutory prospectus for certain offerings (notably mutual funds).
Free writing prospectus (FWP) — Rule 164: written offer that supplements/follows the statutory prospectus; permitted post-filing.
Official Statement (OS): municipal disclosure document — equivalent of a prospectus; preliminary OS (POS) used before pricing.
Program disclosure document: used for DPPs and certain structured products.
Required §23 legend: "These securities have not been approved or disapproved by the SEC..."
Delivery requirements: full prospectus at or before confirmation of sale; aftermarket delivery per Rule 174 (25/90 days).
rules: Securities Act of 1933 §10 — prospectus content rules.
Securities Act of 1933 §23 — disclaimer requirement; misrepresenting SEC review is unlawful.
17 CFR 230.431 — summary prospectus.
17 CFR 230.164 — post-filing free writing prospectus.
MSRB Rule G-32 — underwriter must deliver Official Statement to customers in primary offerings of municipal securities; deemed-final OS required prior to award.
MSRB Rule G-11 — primary offering practices (priority of orders, syndicate operations, allocations).
mnemonics: "RHSF" — Red Herring (preliminary) → Statutory Final prospectus.
"25/90" — Rule 174 aftermarket prospectus delivery: 25 days listed IPO, 90 days unlisted IPO.

sections.title: 5. Secondary Market Structure: Markets I–IV
sections.overview: The secondary market is where existing securities trade between investors after the primary offering; the issuer is not a party to these trades and receives no proceeds. The market is segmented into four overlapping structural categories.
key_concepts: First market — exchange-listed securities traded ON the exchange (e.g., NYSE listed stocks traded on NYSE).
Second market — unlisted securities traded OTC (over-the-counter) through dealer networks; includes OTCBB legacy, OTC Pink, OTCQB, OTCQX.
Third market — exchange-LISTED securities traded OTC (off-exchange) by broker-dealers.
Fourth market — direct institution-to-institution trading via ECNs (Electronic Communication Networks) without broker-dealer intermediation.
Exchange ("auction market"): centralized, price-time priority, designated market makers (DMMs); e.g., NYSE.
OTC ("negotiated market"): decentralized dealer market; market makers quote bid/ask; e.g., Nasdaq (now an exchange but historically OTC).
Alternative Trading Systems (ATS) / Dark pools: non-displayed venues; institutional block trading.
Physical vs. electronic markets — most trading today is electronic; physical floor (NYSE) remains for certain auctions and openings.
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §3(a)(1) — defines "exchange."
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §3(a)(4) — defines "broker" (effects transactions for the account of others).
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §3(a)(5) — defines "dealer" (buys/sells for own account as business).
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §12 — securities must be registered to be traded on a national exchange.
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §15 — broker-dealer registration requirement.
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §15A — registration of national securities associations (FINRA).
mnemonics: "1-2-3-4" markets: "Listed-on-Listed / Unlisted-OTC / Listed-OTC / Institution-to-Institution."
"Exchange = Auction; OTC = Negotiated."

sections.title: 6. Secondary Market Participants: Broker vs. Dealer, Market Makers, and Capacity
sections.overview: Firms participate in the secondary market as agents (brokers) on behalf of customers, or as principals (dealers) trading from their own inventory. The capacity in which a firm acts dictates compensation structure and disclosure on the trade confirmation.
key_concepts: Broker (agent capacity): executes trades for customers; earns a COMMISSION; must disclose role on confirmation.
Dealer / market maker (principal capacity): trades from inventory; earns a MARKUP (buys) or MARKDOWN (sells); price includes the spread.
Riskless principal: dealer buys from one customer and simultaneously sells to another; still principal capacity, but the offsetting trades are matched. Must be disclosed.
Introducing broker-dealer: handles customer relationship; clears through another firm.
Clearing broker-dealer: holds customer assets, clears and settles trades, sends confirms/statements.
Prime broker: provides consolidated clearing/financing to hedge funds and large institutions trading with multiple executing brokers.
Market maker: continuously quotes two-sided bids and offers in specific securities; provides liquidity.
Designated Market Maker (DMM): NYSE specialist successor; maintains fair and orderly market in assigned securities.
Trader: takes proprietary positions for the firm's account.
Custodian: holds customer assets in safekeeping.
Transfer agent: maintains record of registered owners; processes transfers, issues certificates.
Trustee: enforces bond indenture on behalf of bondholders.
DTCC (Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation): central depository / clearing for equities and corporate/municipal bonds.
OCC (Options Clearing Corporation): issuer and guarantor of all listed options contracts.
NSCC / FICC: DTCC subsidiaries clearing equities and fixed income respectively.
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §3(a)(4) and §3(a)(5) — broker and dealer definitions.
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §15 — broker-dealer registration and SRO membership.
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §15A — FINRA as registered national securities association.
FINRA Rule 5250 — payments for market making prohibited (no payments from issuers to BDs to make a market in their security).
FINRA Rule 2266 — SIPC disclosure required to new customers at account opening, in writing.
FINRA Rule 2269 — disclosure of participation/interest in a primary or secondary distribution.
MSRB Rule G-34 — CUSIP, new issue, and market information requirements for municipal securities.
formulas: Markup = Sale Price to Customer − Dealer's Cost (principal trade)
Markdown = Dealer's Cost − Purchase Price from Customer (principal trade)
Commission = Agent fee charged on top of execution price (broker capacity)
Spread = Ask − Bid
mnemonics: "BAD CoM" — Broker = Agent = Commission; Dealer = Principal = Markup.
"DTCC clears stocks; OCC clears options."

sections.title: 7. Quotes & Order Types
sections.overview: A quote shows the price at which a market maker is willing to buy (bid) and sell (ask) a security, along with the size; customer orders specify how and when a trade should be executed. Mastery of order types is a core SIE skill.
key_concepts: Bid: price at which a dealer/market will BUY (customer sells at bid).
Ask / Offer: price at which a dealer/market will SELL (customer buys at ask).
Spread = Ask − Bid (dealer's gross profit).
Size: number of shares (round lots) available at the quoted bid and ask.
Firm quote: dealer must trade at the quoted price for the stated size.
Subject (nominal) quote: indicative only; not actionable.
Workout quote: approximate; subject to negotiation due to illiquidity.
Inside market: highest bid + lowest ask across all market makers (NBBO — National Best Bid and Offer).
Market order: execute immediately at best available price; guarantees execution, not price.
Limit order: buy at limit price or LOWER; sell at limit price or HIGHER; guarantees price (if filled), not execution.
Stop order (stop-loss): becomes a MARKET order when stop price is touched/triggered. Buy stops placed ABOVE market; sell stops BELOW market.
Stop-limit order: becomes a LIMIT order when stop is triggered; risk of no execution if market moves through limit.
Day order: cancelled at end of trading day if unfilled (default).
GTC (Good-Til-Cancelled): remains open until executed or cancelled (firms typically refresh periodically).
Fill-or-Kill (FOK): execute entire order immediately or cancel.
Immediate-or-Cancel (IOC): execute any portion immediately, cancel remainder.
All-or-None (AON): execute in full or not at all; no immediacy required.
Not-Held (NH): gives floor broker discretion over time/price; not held to specific execution.
Market-on-Close (MOC) / Limit-on-Close (LOC): executed at/near the closing price.
rules: FINRA Rule 5250 — no payments to induce market making.
Order audit-trail reporting is via the Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT) under FINRA Rule 6800 Series (OATS was retired 9/1/2021).
formulas: Spread = Ask − Bid
Inside Market (NBBO) = MAX(all bids) and MIN(all asks)
Buy Stop Trigger: market price ≥ stop price → becomes market buy
Sell Stop Trigger: market price ≤ stop price → becomes market sell
mnemonics: "BLISS" — Buy Limits & Sell Stops are placed BELOW the current market; Sell Limits & Buy Stops are placed ABOVE. (Buy Limit / Sell Stop = below; Sell Limit / Buy Stop = above.)
"MIT — Market guarantees execution; Limit guarantees price."
"FOK = all now; IOC = some now; AON = all whenever."

sections.title: 8. Trade Settlement & Clearing
sections.overview: Settlement is the exchange of cash for securities after a trade. The standard regular-way settlement for corporate stocks, corporate bonds, and municipal bonds is T+1 (effective May 28, 2024). Different products and trade types have different settlement conventions.
key_concepts: Regular-way settlement — corporate stocks, corporate bonds, municipal bonds: T+1 (one business day after trade date).
U.S. Treasury securities and listed options: T+1 (next business day).
Equity option EXERCISE: resulting stock delivery settles T+1 (aligned with the equity T+1 cycle, effective 5/28/2024).
Index option exercise: settles next business day in CASH (intrinsic value).
Cash settlement: same day as trade date (T+0); used by mutual agreement.
When-issued (WI): settles when the security is actually issued (used for new Treasury auctions, stock splits, new corporate issues).
Seller's option: settlement date negotiated by parties, typically 2–60 days.
Ex-dividend date (regular-way): SAME business day as record date under T+1 settlement (changed from one day before record date under T+2).
Trade date (T): date the order is executed.
Settlement date: date payment and securities change hands.
Good delivery: securities delivered in transferable form (proper endorsement, round-lot multiples for stock).
DVP (Delivery vs. Payment) / RVP (Receipt vs. Payment): institutional settlement with simultaneous exchange.
Clearance: NSCC (equities/corporates), FICC (governments/MBS), OCC (options). DTC is the central depository for book-entry securities.
rules: SEC Rule 15c6-1 (as amended, effective 5/28/2024) — establishes T+1 as the standard settlement cycle.
FINRA Rule 11140 / equivalent — ex-dividend date determination (same business day as record date under T+1).
MSRB Rule G-12 — uniform practice for inter-dealer municipal settlement.
MSRB Rule G-15 — customer confirmation and settlement (municipals).
Order-event reporting: Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT) under FINRA Rule 6800 Series (OATS retired 9/1/2021).
formulas: Regular-way Settlement Date = Trade Date + 1 business day (T+1)
Treasury / Option Settlement = Trade Date + 1 business day
Ex-Dividend Date (regular-way) = Record Date (same business day, under T+1)
Accrued Interest (corp/muni bonds) = 30/360 day count; (Treasuries) = actual/actual
mnemonics: "T+1 for ALL" — stocks, corporate bonds, muni bonds, Treasuries, options ALL now settle T+1.
"Ex = Record" under T+1 (regular-way ex-date is the same day as record date).
"Cash = today; Reg-way = tomorrow; When-issued = whenever it issues."

sections.title: 9. Regulators, SROs, and Investor Protection Bodies
sections.overview: U.S. securities markets are governed by a layered structure: the SEC at the federal level, SROs (FINRA, MSRB, CBOE, exchanges) at the industry level, state regulators (NASAA-coordinated), and protective entities (SIPC, FDIC). Each has defined jurisdiction.
key_concepts: SEC: created by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; enforces federal securities laws; oversees SROs; civil enforcement authority.
FINRA: SRO for broker-dealers; registered under Exchange Act §15A; writes and enforces conduct rules, examines members, administers qualification exams (including the SIE).
MSRB: writes rules for municipal securities dealers and municipal advisors; enforcement by FINRA/SEC (MSRB does not enforce its own rules).
CBOE: SRO for options trading and listings.
Exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq): SROs for listed-securities trading.
State regulators (Blue-sky / NASAA): enforce state-level securities laws; coordinate via the North American Securities Administrators Association.
Federal Reserve: monetary policy; sets Regulation T (initial margin on securities) and discount rate.
U.S. Treasury / IRS: tax policy and Treasury debt issuance.
SIPC: created by SIPA 1970; protects customers of failed broker-dealers up to $500,000 per customer (of which up to $250,000 may be cash). Does NOT protect against market losses.
FDIC: insures bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per insured bank per ownership category. Does NOT cover securities.
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §3(a) — definitions (exchange, broker, dealer, member).
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §12 — registration of securities on national exchanges.
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §15 — broker-dealer registration with SEC; must join SRO.
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §15A — FINRA's status as registered national securities association; rules must prevent fraud, promote just and equitable principles of trade.
FINRA Rule 2266 — written SIPC disclosure to new customers at account opening (with limited exceptions for non-SIPC members).
FINRA Rule 2269 — disclosure of broker-dealer's participation/control in primary or secondary distributions when soliciting purchases.
formulas: SIPC Coverage = up to $500,000 per separate customer (cash sublimit $250,000)
FDIC Coverage = up to $250,000 per depositor per bank per ownership category
mnemonics: "SEC writes the law; FINRA writes the rules; firms write the checks."
"SIPC = Securities (BD failure); FDIC = Deposits (bank failure)."
"500/250" — SIPC: $500K total, $250K cash.

sections.title: 10. Municipal Securities Primary Market & MSRB Rules
sections.overview: Municipal securities are exempt from 1933 Act registration but are governed by MSRB rules administered through FINRA enforcement. The primary distribution process for new municipal issues has its own disclosure document (the Official Statement) and syndicate procedures.
key_concepts: Municipal securities exempt from 1933 Act registration but NOT from antifraud rules (1934 Act §10(b), Rule 10b-5).
Methods of sale: Competitive bid (issuer awards to lowest TIC/NIC bidder; typical for GO bonds) or Negotiated (issuer selects underwriter directly; typical for revenue bonds).
Official Statement (OS): the municipal disclosure document; preliminary OS (POS) used pre-pricing; final OS delivered post-pricing.
Bond Counsel: provides legal opinion on validity and tax-exempt status; opinion appears on or with the bond.
Municipal Advisor: registered fiduciary advising the issuer; cannot also serve as underwriter on same transaction (role conflict).
Syndicate priority of orders (typical): Pre-sale → Group net → Designated → Member.
CUSIP number assigned to each new issue.
Bond Buyer indices and the Bond Buyer 30-Day Visible Supply track upcoming municipal issuance.
rules: MSRB Rule G-11 — primary offering practices; priority of orders and syndicate operations; settlement of syndicate accounts within prescribed periods.
MSRB Rule G-32 — disclosures in connection with primary offerings; underwriter delivers Official Statement to investors; deemed-final OS prior to award.
MSRB Rule G-34 — CUSIP assignment, new-issue, and market information requirements.
formulas: NIC (Net Interest Cost) = Total Interest Payments − Premium (or + Discount), not time-weighted
TIC (True Interest Cost) = discount rate that equates PV of debt service to bond proceeds (time-weighted)
mnemonics: "PGDM" — Pre-sale, Group net, Designated, Member (order priority under G-11).
"G-32 = Give-32" — give the OS to the customer (G-32).
"Competitive = GO; Negotiated = Revenue."
